meta.blurb: Around 1900 a man finds a sealed cave holding tens of thousands of manuscripts. It is one of ten stops, from Chang'an to Venice, on a road that was never one road. Meet the traders and monks who carried silk and paper.
meta.bible: Silk Road: a modern name, invented in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, for a web of land and sea routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean for about two thousand years. Ten stops, mostly from east to west: Chang'an, Dunhuang, Kashgar, Samarkand, Merv, Baghdad, Palmyra, Constantinople, Karakorum, Venice. Chang'an: capital of the Han dynasty, now Xi'an. Emperor Wu: Han emperor who sent Zhang Qian west about 138 BCE. Zhang Qian: Han envoy, captured by the Xiongnu, away more than ten years. Xiongnu: horsemen of the northern frontier. Ferghana: land of famous horses. Sima Qian: Han historian. Silkworm, Cocoon, Caterpillar, Mulberry: how silk is made. Dunhuang: last Chinese oasis before the desert. Taklamakan Desert: the great desert. Mogao Caves: hundreds of Buddhist cave temples near Dunhuang, started about 366. Buddhism, Buddhist, Buddhists, Buddha, Buddhas: religion from India. Wang Yuanlu: Daoist priest who found the sealed cave about 1900. Daoist. Diamond Sutra: Buddhist text printed in 868, oldest dated printed book that survives. Kashgar: oasis city beneath the Pamir mountains. Pamir: high mountains, the roof of the world. Bactrian: two-humped camel. Caravanserai, Caravanserais, Caravan, Caravans: roadside inns and travelling groups of traders. Xuanzang: Chinese monk who returned from India in the 640s with hundreds of texts; Journey to the West: later novel loosely based on his trip. Samarkand: city in what is now Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan. Sogdians, Sogdian: the great merchants of Central Asia. Aurel Stein: explorer who found the Sogdian letters in 1907. Talas: battle of 751; the story that Chinese prisoners taught papermaking is doubted. Timur: conqueror who made Samarkand his capital in the late 1300s. Registan: great square with three tiled buildings. Merv: oasis city in what is now Turkmenistan, among the biggest cities of the 1100s. Turkmenistan. Karakum: desert. Seljuk: ruling dynasty. Buddhists, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, Muslims: faiths of Merv. Tolui: Mongol commander who took Merv in 1221. Genghis Khan: Mongol leader who united the tribes in 1206. Baghdad: city founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur on the Tigris. Abbasid. Tigris. House of Wisdom: scholars' centre in Baghdad, its exact nature debated. Al-Khwarizmi: mathematician of the early 800s; algebra, algorithm. Algebra, Algorithm. Basra: port. Persian Gulf. Indonesia. Belitung wreck: Arab-style ship sunk about 830, with tens of thousands of Chinese ceramics. Monsoon. Palmyra: Syrian desert oasis city, rich in the first three centuries CE. Syria. Euphrates. CE. Tariff of Palmyra: stone list of taxes carved in 137. Pliny the Elder: Roman writer who complained of gold flowing east. Zenobia: queen of Palmyra, rebelled against Rome in the early 270s. Aurelian: Roman emperor who defeated her in 272. Constantinople: now Istanbul, capital of the Byzantine Empire. Byzantine, Byzantium. Justinian: emperor; about 550 two monks are said to have smuggled silkworm eggs in hollow canes (story from Procopius, probably partly true). Procopius. Rus: northern traders. Scandinavia, Sweden, Russia. Karakorum: Mongol capital in Mongolia, built in the 1230s. Mongolia. Mongol, Mongols. Yam: relay stations. William of Rubruck: Flemish friar who reached Karakorum in 1254. Guillaume Boucher: Parisian goldsmith who made the silver tree. Mongke: Great Khan in 1254. Kublai Khan: Mongol ruler of China, moved the capital to Beijing in the 1260s. Venice: city of the lagoon in northern Italy. Italy, Italian, Venetian. Marco Polo: born in Venice about 1254, left in 1271, back in 1295, wrote about his travels with a fellow prisoner; some doubt details. Black Death: plague reaching Europe in the late 1340s. Ottoman, Ottomans: took Constantinople in 1453. Vasco da Gama: reached India by sea in 1498. Portuguese. UNESCO: named a section in 2014 (China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan; thirty-three sites). Persia, Persian, Arabia, Arab, Asia, Asian, Europe, European, China, Chinese, India, Indian, Africa, Roman, Rome, Romans, Mediterranean, Black Sea, Muslim. Peach: persica means Persian. Voice: warm, clear and curious; hedged where historians disagree; no invented numbers or quotes.

beats.scene: Many tracks cross a map of Asia from China to the sea

beats.scene: A merchant hands a bundle of silk to another trader at a desert market
beats.summary: Goods passed from trader to trader like a relay, so few merchants travelled the whole way.

beats.scene: Crowds fill the broad streets of the Han capital Chang'an

beats.summary: The road was people carrying goods and ideas; nobody owned it, and its gifts are still with us.

B1B2: The name Silk Road is quite modern, because it was invented in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. The merchants who walked these routes long ago never heard that name.

In truth there was never a single Silk Road, only a web of many paths and sea routes. Over about two thousand years, they joined China, Central Asia, Persia, Arabia and the lands around the Mediterranean.
Very few merchants ever travelled the whole way from China to Europe. Instead, goods were passed from one trader to the next, like a baton in a race, and each trader added a profit.
In this book we will visit ten stops, starting in China and ending in Italy. Each one is a real place, and each one tells part of the story.
Our first stop is Chang'an, the capital of China's Han dynasty, which is now called Xi'an. About two thousand years ago it was one of the biggest cities in the world.
Silk is the thread that a small caterpillar, the silkworm, spins around itself to make a cocoon. It feeds on mulberry leaves, and one cocoon can give a thread that is hundreds of metres long.
Around 138 BCE, the Han emperor Wu sent an officer named Zhang Qian to look for allies in the west. He was captured by enemy horsemen, the Xiongnu, and he was away from home for more than ten years.
His reports made the emperor curious about the west, and China soon sent more envoys along the same routes. Silk travelled west, while fine horses, grapes and other new goods came back to China.

Dunhuang was the last green oasis in China before the great desert, so travellers stopped here to rest and to fill their water bags. Beyond the town, the road split into a northern path and a southern path around the Taklamakan Desert.

Buddhism came to China from India along these roads, carried by monks and merchants. Near Dunhuang, monks began to carve small temples into a cliff in about the year 366, and later generations added hundreds more.

Every wall inside the caves is covered with paintings of Buddhas, musicians, flying dancers and even trains of camels. Many were paid for by donors, and some of them were probably merchants hoping for a safe journey.

In about 1900, a Daoist priest named Wang Yuanlu found a sealed cave packed with tens of thousands of old manuscripts. Among them was the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text printed in the year 868, the oldest dated printed book that survives.

After weeks in the desert, the northern and southern paths met again at Kashgar, an oasis city at the foot of high mountains. Here travellers rested, sold some of their goods and prepared for the hardest part of the whole journey.
The Bactrian camel, which has two humps, was the lorry of the Silk Road. It could carry heavy loads, survive bitter cold and go for days without a drink.

The Pamir mountains are so high that people have called them the roof of the world. A Chinese monk named Xuanzang crossed them in the 640s on his way home from India, carrying hundreds of Buddhist texts.

Kashgar is still famous for its big weekly market, where people buy and sell animals, fruit, cloth and bread. A caravan trader from long ago would know the sights and smells, though the phones and motorbikes would surprise him.

Samarkand lies in a green valley in Central Asia, in what is now Uzbekistan. Its people, the Sogdians, became the most successful traders on the road, and they set up trading communities from Persia to China.
In 1907, an explorer found a bundle of letters in a ruined watchtower near Dunhuang. Written by Sogdian merchants about 1,700 years ago, some of them were meant for people back in Samarkand.

Paper was invented in China about two thousand years ago, and its secret slowly travelled west. One story says that Chinese prisoners taught the craft in Samarkand after a battle in 751, but historians disagree about it.

In the late 1300s, the ruler Timur made Samarkand his capital and filled it with skilled craftsmen from conquered lands. The blue-tiled domes and arches of the Registan, its great square, were built in the centuries after him.
Merv was an oasis city in what is now Turkmenistan, watered by a river that flows out of the mountains. In the 1100s, it was one of the largest and richest cities in the world.

Merv was home to people of many faiths, and over the centuries the city held Buddhists, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and Muslims. Archaeologists have found the remains of Buddhist, Christian and Muslim buildings among its ruins.
Merv was also known as a city of learning, and scholars travelled there to study in its libraries. Visitors from the time praised its many books, but almost all of them have been lost.

In 1221, a Mongol army captured Merv, and the city suffered terrible destruction. Old chronicles speak of enormous numbers of dead, but historians think these figures are exaggerated, and Merv never regained its former greatness.

The caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 beside the Tigris River, and he planned it as a great round city. Because rivers and roads met there, it quickly became one of the richest trading centres in the world.

In the 800s, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic. Many accounts link this work to the House of Wisdom, although historians still argue about what exactly that place was.
The mathematician al-Khwarizmi did much of his best work in Baghdad in the early 800s. His book on solving equations gave us the word algebra, and his name is the origin of the word algorithm.

Goods also moved by sea, and ships left the port of Basra to sail towards India and China. Around 830, one such ship sank off Indonesia, and divers later found tens of thousands of pieces of Chinese pottery inside it.

Palmyra was an oasis in the Syrian desert, between the Mediterranean coast and the river Euphrates. In the first three centuries CE, caravans made it rich, and its merchants grew famous for guiding and protecting them.

A great stone, carved in the year 137, lists the taxes that traders had to pay at Palmyra. It names goods such as olive oil, perfume and dyed wool, and shows that the city ran its business by clear rules.
Wealthy Romans adored Chinese silk, and they paid very high prices for it. The writer Pliny the Elder complained that huge sums of gold were flowing out of Rome to pay for luxuries from the east.
In the 270s, Queen Zenobia of Palmyra rebelled against Rome and took control of rich lands in Syria and Egypt. The emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272, and Palmyra never regained its old power.
Constantinople, which is now called Istanbul, was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. It stood on a narrow strait between Europe and Asia, so ships and caravans both brought goods to its markets.

According to a famous story, two monks hid silkworm eggs inside hollow walking sticks and carried them to the emperor Justinian in about 550. Historians think it may be partly true, since the Byzantines did begin to make their own silk soon afterwards.
The Byzantine rulers kept tight control of silk-making, and the trade was supervised by officials. Some of the finest purple silks were reserved for the emperor and his family.

Traders from the north, such as the Rus, travelled down Russia's great rivers to reach Constantinople. They sold furs, honey and other goods, and many Arab silver coins have been found as far away as Sweden.
Our ninth stop takes us back east to Mongolia in the 1200s. In 1206, Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes, and his family went on to build the largest land empire in history.

The Mongols built a system of relay stations, called the yam, where riders could change horses and rest. Envoys and officials carried a metal tablet that told local people to give them food, fresh horses and shelter.

In 1254, a friar named William of Rubruck visited Karakorum and described a marvellous silver tree in the palace. It had been made by a goldsmith from Paris, and pipes inside it poured out wine and other drinks.

Rubruck also described a debate, held before the Great Khan Mongke, between Christian, Muslim and Buddhist teachers. The Mongols usually allowed people to follow their own religions, and they liked to hear the ideas of others.
Our last stop is Venice, a city built on small islands in a shallow lagoon in northern Italy. It had almost no farmland, so its people made their living from ships and trade.

The merchant Marco Polo was born in Venice in about 1254, into a family of traders. At seventeen he set out with his father and uncle for Asia, and he did not see Venice again for about twenty-four years.

Marco Polo's book about his journeys described Chinese cities, grand courts and paper money, which amazed European readers. Some scholars doubt parts of his account, but it was copied by hand again and again and read across Europe.

Merchants in Italy found a much safer way to pay for goods that came from far away. Instead of carrying heavy gold, they used letters of credit, so a trader could pay in one city and be repaid in another.

In the 1340s, a terrible disease called the Black Death reached Europe, probably carried by ships from the Black Sea. Many historians believe it spread along trade routes, and it killed perhaps a third of Europe's people or more.
In 1453, the Ottoman Turks captured the city of Constantinople and made it their new capital. In 1498, the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing all the way around Africa.
Large ships could carry far more cargo than any camel train, and ocean trade grew steadily. Land routes did not vanish overnight, however, and many caravans kept crossing Asia for centuries.
Silk was only one small part of everything that travelled along the roads. Religions, stories, inventions and foods moved too, and paper, printing and gunpowder all spread westward from China.

In 2014, UNESCO named a long section of the old road a World Heritage Site, shared by China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. It includes ruined cities, caravan inns and temples that remind visitors of the road's long history.

The Silk Road had no single owner, no single builder and no single map. It was made by thousands of ordinary people, including traders, monks, soldiers and travellers, who carried goods and ideas from one place to another.
C1C2: Nobody who travelled these routes in ancient times ever spoke of a Silk Road, for the name was coined only in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. He wished to describe the caravan paths that carried Chinese silk westward across mountains and deserts, and the label proved so memorable that it has stuck ever since. Yet a name can mislead, and the story we are about to follow is far larger and more tangled than any single road.

In truth there was never one road at all, but a shifting web of tracks, passes and river crossings that changed with the weather, the wars and the rulers of the day. Some of these paths crossed burning deserts, others climbed through snowbound mountains, and several ran along the sea. Over some two thousand years they linked China, Central Asia, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean in a single, slowly moving conversation.

Hardly any merchant ever travelled the entire distance from China to the Mediterranean, which was far too long, too slow and too dangerous for one person to attempt. Instead, bundles of silk and spice passed from trader to trader, like a baton in a relay, with each new owner adding a share of profit. By the time a roll of silk reached its last buyer, its price had grown many times over, which is part of why it seemed so precious.

Because no map can show two thousand years at once, we will travel the old way, stopping at ten places where the story of the roads comes into sharpest focus. We begin in China, wander mostly westward through desert, mountain and river valley, and finish on the lagoon of Venice. At each stop, a single city or a single moment will teach us something that the whole journey could not.

Our journey begins in Chang'an, the capital of the Han dynasty, a walled city of broad avenues and crowded markets that stood where the modern city of Xi'an stands today. Its emperors ruled a realm of many millions, and their palaces were stocked with the finest goods that Chinese workshops could produce. In the centuries that followed, the city would serve as the eastern gateway of the long roads to the west, and a place where foreign faces were a common sight.

Silk is spun by the silkworm, a pale caterpillar that feeds on mulberry leaves and, when fully grown, wraps itself in a cocoon made of a single unbroken thread. That thread may stretch for hundreds of metres, and when it is unwound, twisted and woven, it becomes a cloth that is light, strong and wonderfully smooth. For many centuries the Chinese guarded the secrets of this craft so closely that outsiders could only guess how the glimmering cloth was made.

In about 138 BCE, the Han emperor Wu sent an officer named Zhang Qian on a dangerous mission to the lands beyond the desert, hoping to find allies against the Xiongnu, the powerful horsemen who raided China's northern frontier. Zhang Qian was seized by those very horsemen and held captive for around ten years, yet he never gave up his task. When at last he returned to China, he had seen cities, rivers and kingdoms that the Han court had never known.

Zhang Qian's reports stirred the emperor's curiosity, and before long a steady stream of envoys, traders and gift-bearers was making its way along the routes he had described. Silk flowed westward in ever greater quantities, while the horses of Ferghana, which were admired for their speed and stamina, travelled eastward to the Han court. According to the historian Sima Qian, grapes and alfalfa also reached China in this period, and they were soon growing in the emperor's own gardens.

Dunhuang was the last oasis town on the Chinese side of the great desert, a green island where weary travellers could rest, buy supplies and say a prayer before the unknown. Beyond it, the road divided into two branches, one skirting the northern edge of the Taklamakan Desert and the other hugging its southern rim. One popular story claims that the desert's name means “go in and you will not come out”, though scholars are not certain of the true meaning.

Buddhism travelled to China from India along these very roads, carried in the baggage of monks, pilgrims and merchants who valued its teachings of compassion and calm. Near Dunhuang, a tradition places the first carved cave temple in the year 366, and over the next thousand years generations of artists added hundreds more, cut into a long cliff above a river. Today they are known as the Mogao Caves, and they form one of the richest treasuries of Buddhist art in the world.

Inside the caves, almost every surface is covered with paint: serene Buddhas, hovering musicians, scenes from sacred stories and even long trains of camels, all made by artists who knew the road well. Such works were paid for by donors, who earned spiritual merit by sponsoring them, and some of those donors were probably merchants hoping for a safe journey. The colours have faded in places, yet the walls still glow like a storybook left open for a thousand years.

Around the year 1900, a Daoist priest named Wang Yuanlu, who was looking after the caves, discovered a small chamber sealed about a thousand years earlier and crammed with tens of thousands of manuscripts. Among the scrolls lay the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text printed from carved wooden blocks in the year 868, which is the oldest dated printed book to have survived. The hidden library, written in many languages, gave scholars a priceless view of everyday life along the road.

After weeks of dust and thirst, the two desert branches of the road came together again at Kashgar, an oasis city that sits beneath the snowy wall of the Pamir mountains. Here caravans rested, weary animals were exchanged for fresh ones, and travellers from Persia, India and China swapped news as well as goods. Everyone knew that the hardest part of the journey, the high mountain passes, still lay ahead.

The Bactrian camel, with its two humps and its shaggy winter coat, was the lorry of the ancient world, able to carry a heavy load, endure bitter cold and walk for days on very little water. At night, caravans stopped at caravanserais, sturdy roadside inns built around an open courtyard, where people and animals could sleep behind thick walls. These shelters were placed roughly a day's journey apart, so that a traveller was seldom far from safety.

The Pamir mountains rise so high that travellers called them the roof of the world, and the thin, freezing air made every step a trial. In the 640s, the Chinese monk Xuanzang crossed them on his way home from India, after more than fifteen years away, with hundreds of Buddhist texts packed in his luggage. His journey, which later inspired a famous adventure novel, shows how far a person might go for the sake of an idea.

Kashgar is still known for its great weekly market, where farmers and herders gather to sell sheep, fruit, bread and cloth under a bright, noisy sky. A caravan trader from a thousand years ago would recognise the bargaining, the sudden laughter and the smell of roasting meat, even if the phones and motorbikes would astonish him. The oldest business on the road, it seems, is simply people meeting other people and agreeing a price.

Samarkand lies in a fertile valley in Central Asia, in what is now Uzbekistan, and its position between China, India and Persia made it a natural meeting point. Its people, the Sogdians, grew into the most enterprising merchants of their age, establishing trading communities in towns from the Persian borderlands all the way to China. For several centuries they acted as the brokers of the road, buying from one culture and selling to another.

In 1907, the explorer Aurel Stein found a bundle of old letters in a ruined watchtower near Dunhuang, where they had lain for about sixteen centuries. They had been written in the Sogdian language by merchants working in China, and some were meant for family and partners back in Samarkand. One letter describes a country in turmoil, and the writer's worry about trade, reminding us that the road was a business before it was a legend.

Paper was invented in China some two thousand years ago, and from the beginning it was cheaper and lighter than the silk, bamboo and animal skins that earlier writers had used. One famous story says that Chinese prisoners taught the craft to the people of Samarkand after the battle of Talas in 751, although historians disagree about how much truth it contains. What is certain is that paper mills soon appeared across the Muslim world, and from there the craft moved slowly towards Europe.

In the late 1300s, the conqueror Timur made Samarkand the capital of a vast empire and filled it with architects, tile-makers and craftsmen gathered from the lands that he had overrun. Over the following centuries, his descendants and later rulers raised great schools, tombs and mosques, glowing with blue and turquoise tiles. The Registan, a square framed by three magnificent arched buildings, still stands as a monument to the wealth that the roads once brought.

Merv rose from the Karakum desert in what is now Turkmenistan, a city made possible by a river that was carefully guided into canals and fields. In the 1100s, when it served as a capital of the Seljuk rulers, it was probably one of the largest cities on Earth. Caravans from east and west met in its markets, and its fruit, cotton and silk were famous.

The great roads carried ideas as easily as cargo, and nowhere was this clearer than in Merv, where Buddhists, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and Muslims all made their homes over the centuries. Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of Buddhist and Christian buildings and of many mosques within the same ruined city. Such a mixture was not always peaceful, but it shows how the road brought different beliefs into daily contact.

Merv won a reputation as a city of learning, and its libraries drew scholars from many lands. Travellers who saw them praised the number of volumes on their shelves, though the exact figures in old accounts may well be exaggerated. Almost nothing of those collections survives, which is a reminder of how much of the past has simply vanished.

In 1221, a Mongol army led by Genghis Khan's son Tolui entered Merv, and the damage to the city and its people was devastating. The medieval chroniclers gave huge numbers for the dead, but modern historians consider those figures greatly exaggerated, even though the loss was undoubtedly terrible. Merv never again held its former place, and today its great ruins lie quiet in the desert, protected as a World Heritage Site.

In 762, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the banks of the Tigris and laid it out as a great round city, with high walls and four gates facing the four quarters of his empire. Rivers and caravan roads met there, and within a few decades the city had grown into a centre of trade, learning and government. Goods from India, China, Africa and the Mediterranean flowed through its markets as easily as the river flowed past its walls.

During the 800s, Baghdad's scholars, paid and encouraged by the caliphs, translated Greek, Persian and Indian works on medicine, mathematics and astronomy into Arabic. Tradition links this great effort to an institution called the House of Wisdom, although historians still debate how large it was and exactly how it worked. Many ancient ideas that might have been forgotten were saved, studied and improved in this way, and they later found their way into Europe.

The mathematician al-Khwarizmi, who lived and worked in Baghdad in the early 800s, wrote a book on solving equations whose Arabic title contained the word al-jabr, from which we get algebra. Another of his works, known to us mostly through Latin translations, helped to spread the Indian system of numerals, with its useful zero, across the Muslim world and eventually Europe. His own name, in its Latin form, became the word algorithm, which today describes the instructions that guide every computer.

Not all the traffic went overland, for ships also sailed from Basra, near the head of the Persian Gulf, to India and onward to China, riding the seasonal monsoon winds. In about 830, one such vessel, built in the Arab style, sank off the coast of Indonesia, and when it was found more than eleven centuries later, it held tens of thousands of pieces of Chinese pottery. The wreck shows that the sea routes were as busy and as valuable as the ones that crossed the sand.

Palmyra rose from the Syrian desert as an oasis with a reliable spring, placed halfway between the Mediterranean coast and the Euphrates, where caravans from the east gladly broke their long crossing. In the first three centuries CE, its merchants grew rich by guiding, protecting and financing those caravans, and they spent their wealth on temples, tombs and a magnificent colonnaded street. Its ruins, with their tall pale columns, remain among the most famous in the world.

Carved in 137 and later discovered among the ruins, the Tariff of Palmyra is a stone slab listing the taxes charged on goods passing through the city. Among the items named are olive oil, perfumes and dyed wool, as well as slaves, which is a reminder that the road also carried human beings. Such a document shows that the grand caravans were governed by rules, officials and carefully calculated fees.

Wealthy Romans adored the soft, shimmering cloth that arrived from the east, and they were willing to pay extraordinary prices for it. The writer Pliny the Elder, who disapproved of such luxury, complained that vast sums of gold were draining out of the empire to pay for goods from India, China and Arabia. His grumbling is one of the oldest complaints about the cost of foreign trade, and it has been repeated by critics ever since.

In the early 270s, Queen Zenobia, who ruled Palmyra on behalf of her young son, rebelled against Rome and seized control of much of Syria and Egypt, creating a short-lived empire of her own. The Roman emperor Aurelian marched east and defeated her in 272, and Palmyra, though it survived, never regained its old importance. Zenobia herself, however, is still remembered in the region as a symbol of courage and of fierce pride.

Constantinople, the city we now call Istanbul, was the capital of the Byzantine Empire, the eastern half of the old Roman world, and it sat on a narrow strait where Europe meets Asia. Ships from the Black Sea and the Mediterranean arrived in its harbours, while caravans from the east entered through its land gates. Few cities in history have been so perfectly placed for trade, and for centuries its markets were a feast of silk, spices, furs and gold.

According to the Byzantine writer Procopius, two monks who had lived far to the east hid silkworm eggs in hollow walking sticks around the year 550 and presented them to the emperor Justinian. Whether or not every detail is true, the Byzantine Empire did begin producing its own silk soon afterwards, and the old Chinese monopoly came to an end. It was a quiet theft that changed the economics of an entire trade, and it was achieved with nothing more than a few eggs and a stick.

Silk-making in Byzantium was a closely supervised industry, with guilds, official workshops and strict rules about who might buy and sell the best cloth. Certain rich purple silks were reserved for the emperor and his family, and giving such a gift to a foreign ruler was a way to show friendship and power at once. Even today, scraps of those splendid fabrics, preserved in church treasuries, remind us how much skill went into a single robe.

Traders from the far north, known as the Rus, rowed and dragged their boats down the great rivers of Russia to reach Constantinople, bringing furs, honey and other goods of the northern forests. They returned home with silver and cloth, and large numbers of Arab silver coins have been dug up in Sweden and elsewhere in Scandinavia. Such finds prove that the web of trade stretched even to cold lands where no silkworm could survive.

Our ninth stop takes us back to the east, to the grasslands of Mongolia in the 1200s, where a remarkable change was under way. In 1206, a leader later known as Genghis Khan united the quarrelling Mongol tribes, and within a few decades his family ruled the largest land empire the world has ever seen. Its first great capital, Karakorum, was built on the open steppe, far from any sea.

The Mongols were fierce conquerors, but once they had taken power they worked hard to keep the roads open, and for a time travel across Asia was safer than it had been for a long while. Relay stations known as the yam were set up at regular intervals, where official riders could swap tired horses for fresh ones and carry messages at astonishing speed. Envoys and officials also carried metal tablets, a kind of passport, that ordered local people to supply them with food, animals and shelter.

In 1254, the Flemish friar William of Rubruck, who had travelled for months to reach the Mongol court, described a marvel in the palace of Karakorum: a great silver tree that poured drinks into basins through hidden pipes. It had been made by a goldsmith from Paris named Guillaume Boucher, who had been taken captive and put to work for the khan. The tree shows how Mongol rulers gathered skilled people from every corner of their empire.

Rubruck also described a public debate staged before the Great Khan Mongke, in which Christian, Muslim and Buddhist teachers argued over their beliefs while the khan listened with interest. The Mongols were generally tolerant of religions, so long as the faithful obeyed the law and paid their taxes, and their court became a meeting place of many creeds. Karakorum's moment did not last, however, because when Kublai Khan moved his capital to what is now Beijing in the 1260s, the old steppe city began to fade.

Our last stop is Venice, a city built on islands in a shallow lagoon in northern Italy, where nearly everything had to arrive by boat. With almost no farmland of its own, Venice lived by the sea, and its merchants became expert at buying goods in the eastern Mediterranean and selling them across Europe. Spices, silks, dyes and other luxuries passed through its warehouses, and the fortunes made there paid for palaces, churches and a mighty fleet.

Marco Polo was born into a Venetian family of merchants in about 1254, and when he was seventeen, his father and uncle took him with them on a long trading journey into Asia. Over the following years, he travelled through Persia and across the mountains of Central Asia, and he reached the court of Kublai Khan, the Mongol ruler of China. He did not return to Venice until 1295, after nearly twenty-four years away, and then wrote the book that made his name famous.

Marco Polo's account of his journeys, written down with the help of a fellow prisoner, described the cities, canals and courts of China, as well as stranger marvels such as paper money and black stones that burned. Some scholars have doubted parts of his story, and a few claim that he never reached China at all, yet most historians accept that he travelled far and saw much of what he reported. Because printing had not yet arrived in Europe, the book spread slowly from one hand-copied manuscript to the next, and it fired the imagination of generations of readers.

The great distances of the trade encouraged clever financial tools, and Italian merchants, especially, became skilled at using letters of credit and bills of exchange. With such papers, a trader could hand over money in Venice and have it repaid in another city, without anyone having to carry a heavy and tempting load of coins across dangerous country. These early banking methods, born of the needs of the roads, are distant ancestors of the cheques and card payments that we use today.

In the late 1340s, a deadly plague that we now call the Black Death arrived in Europe, probably carried by ships from the Black Sea ports. Many historians believe it had travelled westward along the same trade routes that carried silk and spice, and it killed perhaps a third or more of the people of Europe. The same networks that spread wealth and ideas, it seems, could also spread suffering.

In 1453, the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople and made it the capital of a growing empire that would control much of the eastern Mediterranean for centuries. Europeans, eager to reach the riches of Asia, increasingly looked to the ocean, and in 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing all the way around Africa. Historians continue to debate how much the Ottoman conquest actually pushed Europeans to the sea, but the new sea route clearly changed the pattern of trade.

A single large ship could carry as much cargo as hundreds of camels, and as sea routes improved, the price of moving goods by water fell. The old land roads did not vanish overnight, for caravans kept crossing Asia for centuries, but their place at the centre of world trade slowly passed to the oceans. Many once-famous oasis towns grew quieter, and some were gradually swallowed by drifting sand.

Silk was only one small part of what moved along the roads, for religions, stories, inventions and foods travelled too, often in the luggage of people who never knew what they were carrying. Paper, printing and gunpowder all spread westward from China, while grapes, glass and new ideas about mathematics flowed in other directions. Even the peach, which came from China, carries a trace of the journey, since its Latin name, persica, means Persian.

In 2014, UNESCO recognised a long section of the old route, running through China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, as a World Heritage Site, with thirty-three places that include ruined cities, tombs, temples and caravan inns. Many other stops on our journey, such as Samarkand, Merv and the Mogao Caves, are also protected on the list. These places allow modern travellers to stand where merchants, monks and messengers once stood, and to feel the great age of the roads beneath their feet.

The Silk Road had no single owner, no single builder and no single map, and that is perhaps the best way to understand it. It was made by countless ordinary people, among them traders, monks, soldiers, craftsmen and curious travellers, who carried goods and ideas from one end of Asia to the other. Every time we write on paper, taste a peach or open a book from a faraway land, we are still enjoying the gifts of those long, slow, remarkable journeys.
